cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: What Are We Now?
cards.instruction: Find out how someone defines the relationship without directly asking for a label.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Before I approve our booking for your sister's wedding, present your room plan. One room or two?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Economy approved. Double bed, or are you requesting twins?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Twins. I don't want to confuse things.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Twins approved. Now the breakfast arrangement: am I sitting with your family, or waiting for you in the lobby? I want that settled before I authorize the booking.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 demands a booking proposal for approval, A3 grants economy while probing beds and A5 approves twins but withholds final authorization pending family placement, hiding relationship inquiry in superior administration.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 cheap one-room answer leaves intimacy open for A3; B4 twins/no confusion leads A5 to test public family inclusion.

relationship.evidence: B2 offers an economic reason and B4 sets a private boundary without a relationship label, giving meaningful uncertain signals.

heightening.evidence: B4 bed answer causes A5 a different social dimension of belonging rather than repeating the same intimacy question.

specificity.evidence: A1 sister wedding and B2 room economy establish logistics; A5 family breakfast versus lobby supplies a readable belonging test.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 refuses to authorize a booking until breakfast belonging is settled, a dry way to conceal the emotional question.
